archetypes.name: Causation versus correlation
archetypes.abstract: Two things varying together need not be cause and effect; a third factor, reverse direction, or coincidence can produce the association without a causal link.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students read the {association} as proof that {proposed cause} produces {proposed effect}, without ruling out {alternative explanation}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Generate at least one confounder or reverse-direction story for every claimed cause.

reasoningMoves: state the association precisely
propose a confounder
ask what evidence would establish direction

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: Given the {association} between {proposed cause} and {proposed effect}, give one {alternative explanation} that does not require a causal link.
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: produces a plausible confounder or reverse-direction account

references: Bransford et al. (2000); standard methods curricula

archetypes.name: Evidence versus claim
archetypes.abstract: A claim is an assertion; evidence is what licenses it; reasoning is the link between them — and the strength of a claim is bounded by the evidence and the warrant, not by confidence.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students restate {claim} more forcefully instead of linking it to {evidence} through {warrant} and naming its {limitation}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Require the explicit chain: claim — because — evidence — which counts because — except when.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students attach {evidence} to {claim} without explaining the {warrant} that makes it relevant.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Ask 'why does this evidence support that claim?' for each pairing.

reasoningMoves: separate the claim from the evidence
state the warrant linking them
name what would weaken the claim

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: For the position on {claim}, identify the {evidence}, the {warrant} connecting them, and one {limitation} that bounds the claim.
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: explicit claim-evidence-warrant chain with a named limitation

references: Toulmin model of argument; Bransford et al. (2000) on disciplinary reasoning

archetypes.name: Model versus reality
archetypes.abstract: A model is a deliberate simplification that keeps some features and discards others; its usefulness depends on whether its assumptions hold for the question at hand.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students treat {model} as reality itself and forget that {discarded features} were left out, so they apply it where the {breaking assumption} fails.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Name the assumptions; find a case where they break and the model misleads.

reasoningMoves: list what the model keeps and discards
state its assumptions
find where it breaks

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: Identify one {discarded features} of {model} and a situation where the {breaking assumption} makes the model misleading.
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: names a real assumption and a case where it fails

references: Box's 'all models are wrong'; Meyer & Land (2003)

archetypes.name: Operationalization
archetypes.abstract: An abstract construct must be turned into a concrete, measurable indicator; the choice of measure shapes — and can distort — what is found.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students equate {measure} with {construct}, forgetting it only captures {what the measure captures} and misses {what it misses}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Hold the construct fixed and compare two different measures of it.

reasoningMoves: separate the construct from its measure
ask what the measure captures and misses
consider an alternative measure

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: Using {measure} for {construct}, what does it capture well and what {what it misses} does it overlook?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: distinguishes the construct from its operationalization

references: Standard research-methods curricula; Shulman (1986) on PCK

archetypes.name: Contested categories
archetypes.abstract: The categories used to sort the world are human-made, historically situated, and contestable; the choice of category is itself an argument with stakes.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students treat {category} as a natural fact rather than a human choice, missing how drawing it to include {what it includes} and exclude {what it excludes} carries {stake of the boundary}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Show the same phenomenon sorted by two different category schemes and ask who benefits.

reasoningMoves: name what the category includes and excludes
ask who drew it and when
identify the stake of the boundary

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: Examine {category}: what does it include and exclude, and what is the {stake of the boundary} for those it sorts?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: treats the category as a contestable choice with consequences

references: Bowker & Star, Sorting Things Out; critical theory pedagogy

archetypes.name: Part and whole interpretation
archetypes.abstract: Understanding a work moves between its parts and the whole: each detail is read in light of the whole, and the whole is revised as details accumulate.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students catalog {part} of {work} without connecting it to the {whole}, producing description instead of an {interpretive claim}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Require each observed detail to earn its place by supporting a claim about the whole.

reasoningMoves: read a detail closely
relate it to the whole work
revise the interpretive claim as evidence accumulates

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: Choose one {part} of {work} and explain what it contributes to an {interpretive claim} about the {whole}.
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: connects a specific detail to an interpretive claim, not mere description

archetypes.name: Source criticism and provenance
archetypes.abstract: A source is evidence about its maker and moment as much as its ostensible subject; who made it, when, why, and for whom shapes what it can support.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students read {source} as a transparent window onto its subject, ignoring how {maker and context} and {intended audience} shape {what it can support}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Ask who made it, when, for whom, and why before asking what it says.

reasoningMoves: establish provenance
read for the maker's position
bound what the source can support

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: For {source}, how do {maker and context} and {intended audience} shape {what it can support} as evidence?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: uses provenance to bound the source's evidentiary reach

archetypes.name: Conservation and balance
archetypes.abstract: A conserved quantity is neither created nor destroyed within a boundary; what enters minus what leaves equals the change inside, so the books must balance.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students let {quantity} vanish or appear inside {system} instead of tracking it through {inputs} and {outputs} so the balance closes.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Force a full accounting: every unit in, out, or stored — nothing unaccounted.

reasoningMoves: draw the boundary
account for every input and output
close the balance

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: Track {quantity} through {system}: with {inputs} and {outputs} given, what must the change inside be for the balance to close?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: conserves the quantity; no unaccounted creation or loss

references: NGSS crosscutting concept: Energy and Matter — conservation

archetypes.name: Marginal analysis
archetypes.abstract: Good decisions weigh the change from one more unit — the marginal benefit against the marginal cost — not the total or the average.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students judge {decision} by the average or total instead of comparing the {marginal benefit} and {marginal cost} of one more {unit}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Walk one unit at a time and compare the next benefit to the next cost.

reasoningMoves: isolate the change from one more unit
compare marginal benefit to marginal cost
stop where they meet

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: For {decision}, should one more {unit} be chosen? Compare its {marginal benefit} to its {marginal cost}.
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: reasons at the margin, not from totals or averages

exemplars.skin: responsiveness of quantity to the next price change

references: Meyer & Land (2003), opportunity cost as a threshold concept

archetypes.name: Optimization under constraint
archetypes.abstract: An objective is maximized or minimized subject to limits; the best feasible choice usually sits at a constraint boundary, not at an unconstrained ideal.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students optimize {objective} as if {constraints} did not exist, proposing an infeasible ideal instead of the best feasible {decision variables}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Force the choice back inside the feasible region and find the boundary optimum.

reasoningMoves: state the objective and the constraints separately
find the binding constraint
name the tradeoff at the optimum

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: Given {constraints}, which choice of {decision variables} best serves {objective}, and what {tradeoff} does it accept?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: respects the constraints and names the tradeoff at the chosen point

exemplars.skin: revenue tradeoff as price changes along demand

references: Meyer & Land (2003), threshold concepts in economics

archetypes.name: Sampling and inference
archetypes.abstract: A conclusion about a population is drawn from a sample; the sample's variability, not just its average, governs how much the conclusion can be trusted.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students treat {sample} as if it were {population}, ignoring that {statistic} carries {uncertainty} from sampling variation.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Resample several times and watch the statistic move; the spread is the uncertainty.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students believe a larger {sample} removes bias in {population}, conflating precision with representativeness.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Show a large but biased sample that is precisely wrong.

reasoningMoves: distinguish the sample statistic from the population parameter
reason about sampling variability
separate bias from variance

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: From {sample}, what can and cannot be concluded about {population}, and how does {uncertainty} limit the claim?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: states the conclusion AND its uncertainty; does not overgeneralize

exemplars.skin: the sample mean across repeated samples
evidence against a null under sampling variation

references: NGSS crosscutting concept: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity

archetypes.name: Staged process
archetypes.abstract: An outcome is produced by an ordered sequence of stages where each depends on the products of the prior; skipping or reordering stages degrades the result.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students treat the {stages} of {process} as an arbitrary checklist, missing the {dependency} that makes order matter and causes {failure if skipped}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Trace what each stage hands to the next; reorder one and predict the failure.

reasoningMoves: name what each stage produces for the next
identify the dependency that fixes the order
predict the failure from skipping a stage

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: In {process}, why must {stages} occur in order — what {dependency} would break and what {failure if skipped} would result if a stage were skipped?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: explains the dependency, not just the sequence

references: NGSS crosscutting concept: Structure and Function; procedural-knowledge pedagogy

archetypes.name: Equilibrium
archetypes.abstract: Opposing processes run at balancing rates so a quantity holds steady; perturb the system and a restoring force returns it toward balance or shifts it to a new equilibrium point.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students treat the equilibrium in {system} as static — nothing happening — when in fact {opposing processes} continue at equal rates.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Show both processes running and equal at balance; perturb and trace the restoring response.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students assume the equilibrium in {system} is desirable or optimal, when it is only stable.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Separate 'stable' from 'good' with a counterexample equilibrium nobody wants.

reasoningMoves: identify the opposing processes
predict the response to a named perturbation
trace the restoring mechanism
ask what would shift the equilibrium point itself

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: If {perturbation} occurs in {system}, what happens to {balanced quantity} immediately, and what happens after {restoring force} acts?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: names the restoring process and distinguishes the immediate from the settled response

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: A student says {system} at equilibrium has 'stopped changing.' Explain what is actually happening to {opposing processes}.
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: identifies continuing opposing processes at equal rates

exemplars.skin: buyers and sellers; price as the balanced quantity

references: NGSS crosscutting concept: Stability and Change

archetypes.name: Feedback loop
archetypes.abstract: An output of a system is routed back to influence its own input; negative feedback damps change toward stability, positive feedback amplifies change away from it.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students hear 'feedback' in {system} as ordinary cause-and-effect and miss that {output signal} loops back through {feedback path} to change {effect on input}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Draw the loop explicitly and follow one signal all the way around it.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students assume positive feedback in {system} is beneficial, when it names amplification regardless of whether the outcome is desirable.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Give a harmful positive-feedback example (runaway) alongside a helpful one.

reasoningMoves: trace one signal around the loop
classify the loop as damping or amplifying
predict long-run behavior from the loop sign

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: In {system}, follow {output signal} through {feedback path} and explain its {effect on input}. Is this loop stabilizing or amplifying?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: completes the loop and correctly classifies its sign

references: NGSS crosscutting concept: Systems and System Models
Bransford et al. (2000), How People Learn

archetypes.name: Stock and flow
archetypes.abstract: A stock accumulates or depletes only through its flows; the level changes at the net rate of inflow minus outflow, never instantaneously.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students confuse the level of {stock} with the rate of {inflow}, expecting the level to jump when only the flow changed.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Contrast a bathtub's water level with the faucet's flow rate explicitly.

reasoningMoves: separate the level from its rates
compute net flow
predict the level's trajectory, not its jump

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: If {inflow} exceeds {outflow}, what happens to the {level} of {stock} over time, and what happens the moment the flows become equal?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: distinguishes accumulation over time from instantaneous change

references: NGSS crosscutting concept: Energy and Matter — flows and conservation

archetypes.name: System and boundary
archetypes.abstract: A system is defined by a boundary that separates inside from outside and selectively governs what crosses it; what counts as inside is a modeling choice with consequences.

misconceptionShapes.template: Students picture the boundary of {system} as a solid wall rather than a selective interface that regulates {what crosses}.
misconceptionShapes.corrective: Show selective transport: some things cross freely, others not, some only with help.

reasoningMoves: name what the boundary lets through
ask what the chosen boundary excludes
test how conclusions change if the boundary moves

taskSchemas.stemTemplate: Describe how the boundary of {system} regulates {what crosses}. What does this boundary exclude?
taskSchemas.rubricFocus: treats the boundary as selective, not impermeable

exemplars.skin: phospholipid bilayer as the selective boundary

references: NGSS crosscutting concept: Systems and System Models
